dropped.reason: Ambiguous answer: the school accepted both B (4) and C (5) because the question ('how many chain isomers does hexane have?') does not say whether hexane itself is counted.

Flawed: the 'correct' option relies on the Lucas test but the question gives only anhydrous ZnCl2 (no HCl), a test that is outside the syllabus; the intended answer cannot be justified from the information given.

questions.question: A $500$ mL solution of dichromate ions and chromate ions at equilibrium is described by the equation $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons2\text{CrO}_4^{2-}(aq)+2\text{H}^+(aq)$ (dichromate is orange, chromate is yellow). Which of the following best describes the effect of adding 5 drops of concentrated potassium hydroxide solution to the system?
questions.answer: Adding $\text{OH}^-$ removes $\text{H}^+$ by neutralisation ($\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{O}$), so $[\text{H}^+]$ decreases. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts right to replace the $\text{H}^+$, so $[\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}]$ decreases and $[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}]$ increases, and the solution becomes more yellow (C).
options: $[\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}]$ decreases, $[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}]$ increases, $[\text{H}^+]$ increases; the solution becomes more yellow
No change in any concentration; no colour change
$[\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}]$ decreases, $[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}]$ increases, $[\text{H}^+]$ decreases; the solution becomes more yellow
$[\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}]$ increases, $[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}]$ decreases, $[\text{H}^+]$ decreases; the solution becomes more orange

questions.question: The molar solubility of barium phosphate is $6.58\times10^{-3}\ \text{g L}^{-1}$ of water at $25^\circ\text{C}$. Calculate the $K_{sp}$ for barium phosphate at the given temperature.

Exactly $2.0$ mol $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ is placed in an empty $1.0$ L container and is allowed to reach equilibrium as per the equation $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$. If at equilibrium the $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ is $20\%$ dissociated, what is the value of the equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) for the reaction under these conditions?
questions.answer: $20\%$ of $2.0$ mol dissociates, so $0.40$ mol $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ reacts: $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]=1.6$ M and $[\text{NO}_2]=2\times0.40=0.80$ M. $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{NO}_2]^2}{[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]}=\dfrac{0.80^2}{1.6}=0.40$ (A).

questions.question: Silver acetate, $\text{AgCH}_3\text{COO}(s)$, crystals are in equilibrium with a saturated solution. Which of the following would cause more $\text{AgCH}_3\text{COO}(s)$ to dissolve?
questions.answer: $\text{AgCH}_3\text{COO}(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)$. Silver nitrate and sodium acetate add a common ion ($\text{Ag}^+$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$), shifting the equilibrium left so less dissolves. Evaporating water from a saturated solution with solid present just deposits more solid; the saturated concentrations stay the same. HCl removes ions from the solution: $\text{H}^+$ reacts with $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ to form the weak acid $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, and $\text{Cl}^-$ precipitates $\text{Ag}^+$ as AgCl, so the equilibrium shifts right and more solid dissolves (D).
options: The addition of a few crystals of silver nitrate.
The evaporation of some water from the solution with no temperature change.
The addition of a few crystals of sodium acetate.
The addition of a few drops of hydrochloric acid.

questions.question: $10.0$ mL of $1.00\times10^{-5}$ M $\text{AgNO}_3$ and $30.0$ mL of $2.00\times10^{-4}$ M NaCl are mixed. $K_{sp}(\text{AgCl})=1.8\times10^{-10}$. Which one of the following is correct?
questions.answer: Total volume $=40.0$ mL. $[\text{Ag}^+]=\dfrac{1.00\times10^{-5}\times10.0}{40.0}=2.5\times10^{-6}$ M and $[\text{Cl}^-]=\dfrac{2.00\times10^{-4}\times30.0}{40.0}=1.5\times10^{-4}$ M. $Q_{sp}=(2.5\times10^{-6})(1.5\times10^{-4})=3.75\times10^{-10}>K_{sp}=1.8\times10^{-10}$, so a precipitate forms (A).

questions.question: Which of the following is a conjugate acid/base pair that can act as a buffer?
questions.answer: A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and its conjugate acid). $\text{NH}_4^+/\text{NH}_3$ is such a pair (C). $\text{HNO}_3$ is a strong acid so $\text{NO}_3^-$ is a negligible base; $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ and $\text{PO}_4^{3-}$ differ by three protons so are not a conjugate pair; $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ and $\text{SO}_3^{2-}$ are not a conjugate pair.

questions.question: Consider the hydrolysis equation $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)$. Which of the following are conjugate acid-base pairs? i. $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$; ii. $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$; iii. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{OH}^-$; iv. $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$.
questions.answer: A conjugate pair differs by one proton. $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ (base) gains $\text{H}^+$ to form $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$ (acid), so ii is a pair. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (acid) loses $\text{H}^+$ to form $\text{OH}^-$ (base), so iii is a pair. i and iv link a base with an acid from the other pair, so they are not conjugate pairs (B).

questions.question: Which of the following equation/s demonstrate/s the Arrhenius model of acids and bases? i. $\text{HCl}(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)$; ii. $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$; iii. $\text{KOH}(aq)\rightarrow\text{K}^+(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)$; iv. $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_3^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4(aq)$.
questions.answer: In the Arrhenius model an acid is a substance that produces $\text{H}^+$ in water and a base is a substance that produces $\text{OH}^-$ in water, by dissociation. i (HCl produces $\text{H}^+$) and iii (KOH produces $\text{OH}^-$) fit. ii and iv involve proton transfer to or from water or another species, which is the Brønsted–Lowry model (D).

questions.question: A chemist prepares solutions of nitrous acid and hydrocyanic acid that have the same concentration. The $K_a$ values are: nitrous acid ($\text{HNO}_2$) $4.6\times10^{-4}$ and hydrocyanic acid (HCN) $6.17\times10^{-10}$. Which of these two acids is stronger and which has the higher pH?
questions.answer: A larger $K_a$ means a greater extent of ionisation, so nitrous acid is the stronger acid. At the same concentration it produces more $\text{H}^+$, so it has the lower pH, and the weaker acid, hydrocyanic acid, has the higher pH (B).
options: Stronger: nitrous acid; higher pH: nitrous acid
Stronger: nitrous acid; higher pH: hydrocyanic acid
Stronger: hydrocyanic acid; higher pH: hydrocyanic acid
Stronger: hydrocyanic acid; higher pH: nitrous acid

questions.question: Which of the following statements about pure water are correct? i. Pure water is a weak electrolyte that undergoes self-ionisation. ii. The equilibrium constant for the ionisation of pure water at $25^\circ\text{C}$ is $1.00\times10^{-14}$. iii. Pure water ionises completely at $25^\circ\text{C}$, hence $[\text{H}^+]=[\text{OH}^-]$. iv. The ionisation of pure water produces twice as many hydrogen ions as hydroxide ions.
questions.answer: Water self-ionises to a very small extent, $2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)$, so it is a weak electrolyte (i true), and $K_w=[\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]=1.00\times10^{-14}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$ (ii true). It does not ionise completely (iii false) and each ionisation gives one $\text{H}^+$ and one $\text{OH}^-$, so they are in equal amounts (iv false) (A).

questions.question: The structure of methylbutyl acetate is shown. What is the functional isomer of methylbutyl acetate?
questions.answer: Methylbutyl acetate is an ester with molecular formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$. A functional group isomer has the same molecular formula but a different functional group. Option A is heptanoic acid, $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$, a carboxylic acid (a functional group isomer of an ester). B and C are also $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$ esters, so they are chain/position isomers (same functional group), and D is a $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$ ketone with a different molecular formula (A).

questions.question: Which of the following compounds is 1,2-dichloro-2-pentene?
questions.answer: 1,2-dichloro-2-pentene is $\text{ClCH}_2-\text{C(Cl)}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$: a five-carbon chain with the double bond between carbons 2 and 3, a chlorine on carbon 1 ($\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) and a chlorine on carbon 2. Option D has $\text{C(Cl)}(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl})=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (D). A has the chlorines on the same carbon-pair of a 2-pentene (2,3-dichloro), B is a different chain and C is a four-carbon chain.

questions.question: In a $^{13}$C-NMR, how many carbon environments would the compound shown present?
questions.answer: The compound is $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, with 9 carbons. The two methyl groups of the isopropyl group are equivalent (one environment), and every other carbon is different: $\text{CH}_3$ (on the double bond), $=\text{CH}$, $=\text{C}$, $\text{CH}$ of the isopropyl, the 2 equivalent $\text{CH}_3$, and the $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$ of the propyl group. $9-1=8$ environments (B).

questions.question: The high resolution proton NMR spectrum of chloroethane has two sets of peaks. Both peaks are split. Which of the following correctly describes the splitting pattern that would be observed?
questions.answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$: the $\text{CH}_3$ hydrogens have 2 neighbouring H (on the $\text{CH}_2$), so by the $n+1$ rule they give a triplet; the $\text{CH}_2$ hydrogens have 3 neighbouring H (on the $\text{CH}_3$), so they give a quartet (D).

questions.question: Electromagnetic radiation of a specific wavelength can interact with some molecules and atoms by promoting electrons at a low energy level to higher energy levels. Which pair of analytical techniques relies on the measurement of these electronic transitions?
questions.answer: Atomic absorption spectroscopy (valence electrons in atoms absorbing characteristic wavelengths) and UV-visible spectroscopy (electronic transitions in ions and molecules) both rely on electron transitions between energy levels. Infrared spectroscopy measures bond vibrations, NMR measures nuclear spin transitions, and mass spectrometry measures the mass-to-charge ratio of ions (A).
options: Atomic absorption spectroscopy and UV-visible spectroscopy
Infrared spectroscopy and atomic absorption spectroscopy
Proton NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry

questions.question: A chemist suspected that an impure copper lump contained a significant amount of cobalt. Cobalt would be oxidised to $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ions which would remain in the electrolyte solution. The spectrogram shown gives the results of an analysis conducted on the solution. The two ions absorb at distinctly different wavelengths. Which analytical technique was used to perform this analysis?
questions.answer: The spectrogram shows absorbance against wavelength (about 400–1100 nm) with broad absorption bands from coloured ions in solution ($\text{Co}^{2+}$ near 500 nm, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ near 800 and 1000 nm). This is a UV-visible (visible region) absorption spectrum (C). AAS measures atoms at a fixed characteristic wavelength, mass spectrometry plots abundance against $m/z$, and IR plots against wavenumber.

questions.question: An atomic absorption spectrometer can be used to determine the level of copper in soils. The calibration curve shown plots the absorbance of four standard copper solutions against the concentration of copper ions in ppm. The concentrations of copper ions in the standard solutions were $1.0$, $2.0$, $3.0$ and $4.0\ \text{mg L}^{-1}$ ($1\ \text{mg L}^{-1}=1$ ppm). The concentration of copper in a test solution can be determined most accurately from the calibration curve if it is between:
questions.answer: A calibration curve is reliable only by interpolation within the range of the standards actually measured (1.0 to 4.0 ppm). Outside this range the line is an extrapolation and the response may not be linear (C).

questions.question: An atomic absorption spectrometer was calibrated with four standard copper solutions of $1.0$, $2.0$, $3.0$ and $4.0\ \text{mg L}^{-1}$ (see the calibration curve). If the sample solution gave an absorbance reading of $0.40$, what would be the concentration, in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$, of copper ions in the solution?
questions.answer: From the calibration curve an absorbance of $0.40$ corresponds to $2.5$ ppm, i.e. $2.5\ \text{mg L}^{-1}=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{g L}^{-1}$. $c=\dfrac{2.5\times10^{-3}}{63.55}=3.9\times10^{-5}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ (B).

questions.question: A saturated solution of lead chloride has a $K_{sp}$ value of $1.70\times10^{-5}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$. Calculate the concentration of $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ ions in a solution after $20.0$ mL of $0.150\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ HCl is added to $30.0$ mL of a saturated lead chloride solution.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** $\text{PbCl}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{Cl}^-(aq)$, $K_{sp}=[\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^2$.

The HCl is diluted to a total volume of $50.0$ mL: $[\text{Cl}^-]_{\text{from HCl}}=\dfrac{0.150\times0.0200}{0.0500}=0.0600$ M. This is a common ion, so the solubility of $\text{PbCl}_2$ is reduced. Let $x$ be the $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ concentration at equilibrium: $[\text{Cl}^-]=0.0600+2x$.

$K_{sp}=x(0.0600+2x)^2=1.70\times10^{-5}$.

*School's approach (neglecting $2x$):* $[\text{Pb}^{2+}]=\dfrac{1.70\times10^{-5}}{(0.0600)^2}=4.72\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

(Note: the school's guidelines justify neglecting $2x$ because $K_{sp}<10^{-4}$, but here $2x\approx0.0094$ is not negligible compared with $0.0600$ (about 16%). Solving $x(0.0600+2x)^2=1.70\times10^{-5}$ without the approximation gives $x=3.7\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$. The school's key answer is $4.72\times10^{-3}$ M.)

questions.question: Bromomethane reacts with hydroxide to form methanol and bromide ion: $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}(g)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)+\text{Br}^-(aq)$. Two reaction vessels containing the equilibrium mixture were heated to two temperatures, $30^\circ\text{C}$ and $80^\circ\text{C}$, and the concentration of $\text{Br}^-$ was recorded. The results are shown in the graph. State whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** Exothermic. At the higher temperature ($80^\circ\text{C}$) the equilibrium concentration of $\text{Br}^-$ (a product) is lower than at $30^\circ\text{C}$, so raising the temperature shifted the equilibrium to the left, favouring the endothermic reverse reaction. The forward reaction is therefore exothermic. (The $80^\circ\text{C}$ reaction reaches its plateau faster because the rate is higher.)

questions.question: Bromomethane reacts with hydroxide to form methanol and bromide ion: $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}(g)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)+\text{Br}^-(aq)$. The graph shows the concentrations of three of the species involved when they are at equilibrium at constant temperature. Excess silver nitrate, $\text{AgNO}_3$, solution was added to the equilibrium mixture at time $t_1$. Sketch the impact that the addition of silver nitrate would have on each of the species in the solution. Explain the shape of the graph you have drawn.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** (See the graph.) Before $t_1$ all three concentrations are constant (equilibrium). At $t_1$ the $[\text{Br}^-]$ drops almost instantly to (nearly) zero and stays there, while $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ gradually increases and $[\text{CH}_3\text{Br}]$ gradually decreases, each levelling off at a new constant value.

*Explanation:* $\text{AgNO}_3$ dissociates to give $\text{Ag}^+$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$. $\text{Ag}^+$ reacts with $\text{Br}^-$ to form the very insoluble precipitate AgBr ($\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{Br}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{AgBr}(s)$; AgBr is less soluble than AgOH, which has a larger $K_{sp}$, so it forms first). Because the $\text{Ag}^+$ is in excess, essentially all the $\text{Br}^-$ is removed, so $[\text{Br}^-]$ falls sharply to about zero and remains there as any new $\text{Br}^-$ formed is continually removed. By Le Chatelier's principle, the system opposes the decrease in $[\text{Br}^-]$ by shifting to the right (forward reaction), so $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$ (and $\text{OH}^-$) are used up, causing $[\text{CH}_3\text{Br}]$ to decrease gradually, and $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ is formed, so $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ increases gradually. The changes are gradual (not instant) since they depend on the rate of the forward reaction, and the concentrations level off (straight lines) when the forward and reverse rates are equal again at the new equilibrium position.

questions.question: Methanol is a useful fuel that can be manufactured from biogas as represented by the equation $\text{CO}(g)+2\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$, $\Delta H<0$. Explain, with reference to ONE key principle, how reaction temperature and pressure can affect the yield of methanol from biogas.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** Using Le Chatelier's principle (when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to partially counteract the change):

*Temperature:* $\Delta H<0$, so the forward reaction is exothermic. Decreasing the temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction (which releases heat to oppose the cooling), so the equilibrium shifts right and the yield of methanol increases. Increasing the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, decreasing the yield.

*Pressure:* The reactant side has 3 mol of gas ($1\ \text{CO}+2\ \text{H}_2$) and the product side has 1 mol of gas. Increasing the pressure (by decreasing the volume) favours the side with fewer moles of gas, the forward reaction, to reduce the pressure, so the yield of methanol increases. Decreasing the pressure decreases the yield.

questions.question: For the synthesis of methanol, $\text{CO}(g)+2\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$, $0.840$ mol of carbon monoxide, CO, and $0.325$ mol of hydrogen, $\text{H}_2$, were allowed to reach equilibrium in a $500$ mL container. At equilibrium the mixture contained $0.150$ mol of methanol. Calculate the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, of the synthesis of methanol.

Two solutions of equal concentration were prepared: one of ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, and one of ammonium chloride, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$. $\text{p}K_a(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})=4.76$ and $\text{p}K_a(\text{NH}_4^+)=9.24$. Compare the pH and electrical conductivity of both solutions of equal concentration. Your answer should include relevant equation(s).
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** *pH.* Ethanoic acid has the lower $\text{p}K_a$ (4.76) and so the larger $K_a$ ($1.74\times10^{-5}$ compared with $5.75\times10^{-10}$ for $\text{NH}_4^+$). $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$ ionises to a much greater extent than $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(aq)\rightarrow\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)$ followed by $\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. At the same concentration $c$, $[\text{H}^+]\approx\sqrt{K_ac}$ is therefore greater for ethanoic acid, so the ethanoic acid solution has the lower pH (e.g. at $0.1$ M: pH 2.88 vs 5.12). Both are acidic.

*Electrical conductivity.* Conductivity depends on the concentration of mobile ions. Ethanoic acid is a weak acid that is only about 1% ionised, so most of it remains as molecules. Ammonium chloride is a soluble ionic compound that dissociates completely into $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions (only a tiny fraction of the $\text{NH}_4^+$ then reacts with water), so the $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ solution contains a much higher concentration of ions and has the higher conductivity.

(Note: the school's sample answer says that the ethanoic acid solution would be the more conductive because it produces more $\text{H}^+$. This overlooks the complete dissociation of the salt $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ into ions, which is the main reason for its conductivity.)

questions.question: Emilio made the following statement about the solubility of ammonium chloride in water at varying temperatures (graph shown): 'Ethanoic acid is not soluble in water, it only ionises whereas ammonium chloride, irrespective of the mass, is 100% soluble in 100 g of water'. Assess the validity of Emilio's statement regarding the solubility of ethanoic acid and ammonium chloride, using your own knowledge and the stimulus provided. Include a labelled diagram to support your answer.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** Emilio's statement is not valid for either compound.

*Ethanoic acid.* Ethanoic acid is soluble in water (it is miscible). Its molecules contain a polar carbonyl ($\text{C=O}$) group and a polar hydroxyl ($\text{O-H}$) group, so the $\text{O-H}$ hydrogen can form hydrogen bonds with the oxygen atoms of water, and the oxygen atoms of the acid can accept hydrogen bonds from the hydrogen atoms of water ($\text{O-H}\cdots\text{O}$, strong intermolecular attractions). The non-polar $\text{CH}_3$ 'tail' is short, so these attractions are enough for it to dissolve. Dissolving is a physical process (hydrogen bonds between molecules); it is separate from ionisation, in which a small fraction of the dissolved molecules transfer a proton to water, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. So the claim that it is 'not soluble, it only ionises' is wrong.

*Ammonium chloride.* $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ is an ionic compound that dissolves because ion–dipole attractions between $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions and the polar water molecules (the $\delta^-$ oxygen attracted to $\text{NH}_4^+$, the $\delta^+$ hydrogens to $\text{Cl}^-$) overcome the ionic bonds in the lattice. However, the graph shows that its solubility is limited and depends on temperature (about $29\ \text{g}$ per 100 g of water at $0^\circ\text{C}$, rising to about $65\ \text{g}$ per 100 g at $70^\circ\text{C}$). Once that mass has dissolved at a given temperature the solution is saturated: undissolved solid is in dynamic equilibrium with its dissolved ions, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)$, and no more dissolves. So it is not '100% soluble irrespective of the mass'.

questions.question:
Benzoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$) is a weak acid. The benzoic acid content of products can be determined by titration with sodium hydroxide. The salt produced in the titration reaction is sodium benzoate, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COONa}$. The graph shows a typical acid-base titration curve for benzoic acid and sodium hydroxide. Which of the indicators listed in the following table would be most suitable for use in this titration? Explain your choice.

| Name of indicator | pH range |
|---|---|
| Bromocresol green | 3.8–5.4 |
| Azolitmin | 4.5–8.3 |
| Cresolphthalein | 8.2–9.8 |
| Indigo carmine | 11.4–13.0 |
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** Cresolphthalein. The end point (the colour change of the indicator) should coincide with the equivalence point as closely as possible. On the curve, the equivalence point is at about 50 mL NaOH, in the middle of the steep section, at a pH of about 9 (above 7 as the salt, sodium benzoate, is basic: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}+\text{OH}^-$). Cresolphthalein (pH 8.2–9.8) is the only indicator whose range contains this pH, and the pH changes by several units with one drop of NaOH there, so its colour change occurs at the equivalence point. Bromocresol green and azolitmin change colour in the gradually sloping buffer region, long before the equivalence point, and indigo carmine changes colour only after the steep rise, well after it.

questions.question: The graph shows a typical titration curve for benzoic acid (a weak acid) titrated with sodium hydroxide, in which buffering is observed during the titration. Identify the region of the titration curve in which the buffering occurs.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** The buffer region is the gently sloping section of the curve before the steep rise, from about 5 mL up to about 45 mL of NaOH added (centred on the half-equivalence volume, about 25 mL, where $\text{pH}=\text{p}K_a$). In this region the pH changes only slightly as NaOH is added, unlike the very steep rise around the equivalence point (about 50 mL) and the flat region after it (past about 55 mL).

questions.question: Benzoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$) is titrated with sodium hydroxide and buffering is observed in the region of the titration curve before the equivalence point. Define the term 'buffer' and explain why there is a buffer present in this region. Include an equation to support your explanation.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** A buffer is a solution containing a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) in comparable amounts, which resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

Before the equivalence point, only part of the benzoic acid has been neutralised by $\text{NaOH}$ ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}+\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_2\text{O}$), so the solution contains both the weak acid $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ and its conjugate base $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-$ (from sodium benzoate), which are in equilibrium: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. When more $\text{OH}^-$ is added, it reacts with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts right (benzoic acid ionises) to replace the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, so the pH changes only slightly. When more benzoic acid has been consumed than remains (i.e. around the equivalence point) there is no longer enough weak acid to replace the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and the pH rises sharply.

questions.question: When bubbled into water, hydrogen fluoride gas, HF(g), reacts with water to form a weakly acidic solution. Write a chemical equation to show the reaction of hydrogen fluoride gas with water.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** $\text{HF}(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{F}^-(aq)$ (a reversible arrow, as HF is a weak acid).

questions.question: Hydrogen fluoride gas dissolves in pure nitric acid as follows: $\text{HNO}_3(aq)+\text{HF}(g)\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{NO}_3^+(aq)+\text{F}^-(aq)$. State, with a reason, which of the two reactants is acting as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** HF is the Brønsted–Lowry acid. A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton ($\text{H}^+$) donor: HF donates a proton to $\text{HNO}_3$, forming $\text{F}^-$ (its conjugate base), while $\text{HNO}_3$ accepts the proton to form $\text{H}_2\text{NO}_3^+$ (so $\text{HNO}_3$ acts as the Brønsted–Lowry base).

questions.question: Calculate the pH of a hydrofluoric acid solution of concentration $0.20\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$, given the $K_a=6.8\times10^{-4}$.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** $\text{HF}(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{F}^-(aq)$, $K_a=\dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{F}^-]}{[\text{HF}]}$.

| (M) | HF | $\text{H}^+$ | $\text{F}^-$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.20 | 0 | 0 |
| Change | $-x$ | $+x$ | $+x$ |
| Equilibrium | $0.20-x$ | $x$ | $x$ |

Assuming $x$ is negligible compared with $0.20$: $6.8\times10^{-4}=\dfrac{x^2}{0.20}$, so $x=\sqrt{0.20\times6.8\times10^{-4}}=0.01166$ M $=[\text{H}^+]$. $\text{pH}=-\log_{10}(0.01166)=1.93$.

(Solving the quadratic without the approximation gives $x=0.0113$ M and $\text{pH}=1.95$; the school accepted 1.9 or 1.93.)

questions.question: Glycolic acid (2-hydroxyethanoic acid) is a weak monoprotic acid used in some skincare products. Draw the structural formula of glycolic acid.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** Glycolic acid is $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-COOH}$. Drawn out in full: a carbon atom ($\text{C}_2$, the carboxyl carbon) double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to an $\text{-OH}$ group, and single-bonded to a second carbon ($\text{C}_1$) which carries two hydrogen atoms and a hydroxyl group, $\text{-OH}$:

$$\text{H}-\overset{\text{H}}{\underset{\text{OH}}{\text{C}}}-\overset{\text{O}}{\overset{\|}{\text{C}}}-\text{O}-\text{H}$$

(2 carbons, 3 oxygens, 4 hydrogens: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$.)

questions.question: Glycolic acid (2-hydroxyethanoic acid, $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$) is a weak monoprotic acid. Write the chemical equation to show the acid dissociation of glycolic acid.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{HOCH}_2\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$ (equivalently $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_3^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$).

questions.question: Glycolic acid is a weak monoprotic acid. Sodium glycolate, $\text{NaCH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COO}$, is a soluble salt of glycolic acid. If some solid sodium glycolate is dissolved in a solution of glycolic acid, explain the effect this would have on its pH.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** The acid is in equilibrium: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{HOCH}_2\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. Sodium glycolate dissolves completely to give $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COO}^-$ ions, so the concentration of the glycolate ion (a common ion) increases. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the left to use up some of the extra glycolate ion, so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ decreases. Since $\text{pH}=-\log[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$, the pH of the solution increases.

questions.question: The solubility of glycolic acid ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$) is $1.0\times10^6$ mg per litre at $25^\circ\text{C}$. Calculate the concentration, in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$, of a saturated solution of glycolic acid.

A saturated solution of glycolic acid ($\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$) has a concentration of $13\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ($1000\ \text{g L}^{-1}$). $100$ mL of this saturated solution is spilt onto the floor. What is the minimum mass of sodium carbonate that should be used to neutralise the spill?
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(s)+2\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}(aq)\rightarrow2\text{HOCH}_2\text{COONa}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{CO}_2(g)$ (acid : carbonate $=2:1$).

$n(\text{acid})=1000\ \text{g L}^{-1}\times0.100\ \text{L}\div76.05\ \text{g mol}^{-1}=1.315$ mol (using $13$ M exactly: $1.3$ mol).

$n(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3)=\tfrac12\times1.315=0.657$ mol. $M(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3)=2(22.99)+12.01+3(16.00)=105.99\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

$m=0.657\times105.99=70\ \text{g}$ (2 s.f.). Using the rounded $13$ M gives $n(\text{acid})=1.30$ mol, $n(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3)=0.65$ mol and $m=69$ g, which is the value in the school's sample answer.

questions.question: A colourless volatile liquid compound has a chemical formula of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. It was observed to successfully oxidise in the presence of acidified potassium dichromate. Based on the information provided, what type of compound would the colourless liquid be? Justify your response.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** An aldehyde. Primary and secondary alcohols and aldehydes are oxidised by acidified dichromate, but ketones are not. An alcohol with five carbons would have the formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$ (pentanol, etc.), not $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, and the formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}$ fits aldehydes and ketones. Since a ketone would not be oxidised, the compound must be an aldehyde (oxidised to a carboxylic acid).

questions.question:
A colourless volatile liquid compound has a chemical formula of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. It was observed to successfully oxidise in the presence of acidified potassium dichromate. The mass spectrum, $^{13}$C NMR spectrum and infrared spectrum of the compound are shown, along with the proton NMR data in the table.

| Shift (ppm) | Number of peaks | Peak area ratio |
|---|---|---|
| 0.90 | 3 | 3 |
| 1.35 | 6 | 2 |
| 1.60 | 5 | 2 |
| 2.40 | 3 | 2 |
| 9.20 | 1 | 1 |

Draw and name the unknown compound that is consistent with ALL of the information provided. Justify your answer with reference to the information provided.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** The compound is pentanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ (a straight-chain aldehyde).

*Reactivity and formula.* The compound is oxidised by acidified dichromate and its formula is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ (no $\text{O-H}$ and one degree of unsaturation), so it is an aldehyde (a ketone would not be oxidised).

*Mass spectrum.* The molecular ion peak is at $m/z=86$, which matches the molar mass of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ ($5\times12+10\times1+16=86$). Fragment peaks at $m/z=29$ ($\text{CHO}^+$ or $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+$), $44$ (the base peak, from a rearrangement of the molecular ion, characteristic of an aldehyde) and $57$ ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_9^+$, loss of $\text{CHO}$) are consistent with pentanal.

*$^{13}$C NMR.* There are 5 peaks for 5 carbons, so all five carbon environments are different (an asymmetrical, unbranched structure; the branched isomer 3-methylbutanal would give only 4 peaks). The peak at about $202$ ppm is characteristic of the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde ($190$–$220$ ppm), and there is no peak at $160$–$185$ ppm (ester/acid) or $50$–$90$ ppm (alcohol). The remaining peaks, about $44$, $24$, $22$ and $14$ ppm, are the four sp$^3$ carbons: the $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$ is the furthest downfield and the $\text{CH}_3$ furthest upfield.

*IR.* A strong sharp absorption at about $1720$–$1750\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ is the $\text{C=O}$ stretch of a carbonyl compound (aldehyde, ketone or acid), and absorptions at $2850$–$3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ are $\text{C-H}$ stretches. There is no broad band at $3200$–$3550\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ ($\text{O-H}$, so no alcohol) and no broad band at $2500$–$3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ (carboxylic acid $\text{O-H}$), and no pair of peaks at $3300$–$3500\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ (not an amine). The $\text{C=O}$ with the oxidation test and the $^{13}$C shift identify it as an aldehyde.

*$^1$H NMR.* Five environments, with the peak areas $3:2:2:2:1=10$ H. $0.90$ ppm (3H, triplet): $\text{CH}_3$ next to a $\text{CH}_2$. $1.35$ ppm (2H, sextet): $\text{CH}_2$ with 5 neighbouring H ($\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2$). $1.60$ ppm (2H, quintet): the middle $\text{CH}_2$ with 4 neighbouring H. $2.40$ ppm (2H): the $\text{CH}_2$ next to the carbonyl, deshielded by $\text{C=O}$ (the shift is in the $2.1$–$2.6$ ppm range). $9.20$ ppm (1H, singlet): the aldehyde $\text{CHO}$ proton, very deshielded (the aldehyde range is $9.4$–$10$ ppm), with no resolved coupling.

(Note: strictly, by the $n+1$ rule the $\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ signal should be a quartet and the $\text{CHO}$ signal a triplet; the data give a triplet and a singlet because the coupling between the $\text{CHO}$ proton and the adjacent $\text{CH}_2$ is very small and usually not resolved. The school's marking notes this mismatch but still accepts pentanal.)

questions.question: The reaction pathway shown represents the synthesis of compound E. Only ONE organic product is formed in each step, so no isomeric products are possible. A converts to B with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and heat; B converts to C with $\text{KMnO}_4$ / dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat (reflux); D converts to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ with $\text{Cl}_2$ and heat; $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ converts to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ with $\text{NH}_3$; C and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ react on heating to give E. Name the type of reaction that occurs to convert compound: i) A into B; ii) B into C; iii) C into E; iv) D into $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** i) Addition (hydration). ii) Oxidation. iii) Condensation (amide formation; $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is eliminated as the small molecule). iv) Substitution (halogenation).

questions.question: The reaction pathway shown represents the synthesis of compound E. Only ONE organic product is formed in each step, so no isomeric products are possible. A converts to B with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and heat; B converts to C with $\text{KMnO}_4$ / dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat (reflux); D converts to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ with $\text{Cl}_2$ and heat; $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ converts to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ with $\text{NH}_3$; C and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ react on heating to give E. Draw the chemical structures of compounds A to E.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.**

| Compound | Name | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| A | ethene | $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$ |
| B | ethanol | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ |
| C | ethanoic acid | $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ |
| D | propane | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ |
| E | N-propylethanamide | $\text{CH}_3\text{CONHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ |

A must be ethene: hydration of ethene gives only one alcohol (ethanol), whereas a longer alkene such as propene would give isomeric alcohols. Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid (C). Chlorination of propane gives 1-chloropropane, so D is propane. The acid C reacts with the amine $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ by condensation (loss of $\text{OH}$ from the acid and $\text{H}$ from the amine as water) to give the amide E, $\text{CH}_3\text{C(=O)NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

questions.question: Ethanol (B) is converted to ethanoic acid (C) in the school laboratory using $\text{KMnO}_4$ / dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with heating under reflux. Explain the reaction conditions required to successfully convert compound B to C in the school laboratory. Include a labelled diagram of the apparatus.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** Ethanol is oxidised to ethanal and then to ethanoic acid: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.

- *Excess oxidising agent* ($\text{KMnO}_4$ or $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$): so there is enough to oxidise the ethanol to ethanal and then the ethanal further to ethanoic acid (if the aldehyde were wanted, the alcohol would be in excess).
- *Dilute sulfuric acid:* provides the acidic medium ($\text{H}^+$) required for the oxidising agent to work.
- *Heating under reflux:* ethanol and ethanal are volatile (ethanal boils at $21^\circ\text{C}$), so the mixture is heated in a flask fitted with a vertical (Liebig) condenser; vapours condense and run back into the flask, so the intermediate ethanal stays in the reaction mixture and is oxidised to the acid, which increases the yield. Heating increases the rate of reaction.

*Apparatus (labelled diagram described):* a round-bottomed flask containing the reaction mixture and anti-bumping chips, heated by a heating mantle or a water bath (not a naked flame, as the vapours are flammable), with a vertical condenser fitted to the neck; cooling water enters at the bottom of the condenser and leaves at the top (so the jacket is always full); the top of the condenser is open to the air (never sealed with a stopper, to avoid a build-up of pressure).

questions.question: Consider the reaction pathway shown, drawn by a chemistry student, showing the production of an ester: propene ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) is converted with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ / dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to propan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$); 2-methylpropene is converted with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ / dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to 2-methylpropan-2-ol, which is converted with $\text{H}^+/\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, heat to 2-methylpropanoic acid; the acid and propan-1-ol are then converted with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat (reflux) to the ester propyl 2-methylpropanoate. The student's reaction pathway is riddled with errors. Identify and explain the errors in the student's reaction pathway with reference to ONE key chemistry principle. Support your answer with labelled diagrams.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** *Key principle: Markovnikov's rule* — when $\text{H-OH}$ adds across an unsymmetrical $\text{C=C}$, the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms, so the OH ends up on the more substituted carbon and a major and a minor product form.

*Error 1: hydration of propene.* The major product of the hydration of propene is propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ (OH on the middle carbon, the more substituted carbon), with propan-1-ol as the minor product. The student drew only the minor product (and a mixture would actually form, so a single product cannot be assumed).

*Error 2: hydration and oxidation of 2-methylpropene.* By Markovnikov's rule the major product is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$, a tertiary alcohol. Tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidised by acidified dichromate (there is no hydrogen on the carbon carrying the $\text{OH}$), so the oxidation step shown cannot produce 2-methylpropanoic acid. To make the acid, the primary alcohol 2-methylpropan-1-ol (only a minor hydration product) would be needed.

*Error 3: conditions and reagents.* Oxidation of an alcohol to a carboxylic acid must be done with an excess of acidified dichromate under reflux (the oxidant is $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$/$\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with $\text{H}^+$; the student wrote the formula incorrectly), and the esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol needs conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst and heating under reflux. The student's pathway also combines the two separate branches, treating propan-1-ol as a product of the same sequence, and the tertiary alcohol would not form an ester under these conditions (with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and heat it dehydrates back to the alkene).

*Diagrams:* the major hydration product of propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, and of 2-methylpropene, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-OH}$ (tertiary: carbon bonded to three other carbons and the OH, no H).
